text: A police‑officer may arrest a person without a warrant when the officer has reason to believe the person is liable to be arrested under any of the categories listed in section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. These include: (i) a person who commits a cognizable offence in the officer’s presence; (ii) a person against whom a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion exists of having committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years; (iii) a person against whom credible information shows he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of more than seven years or a death sentence; (iv) a person found in possession of an implement of house‑breaking; (v) a proclaimed offender; (vi) a person found in possession of suspected stolen property; (vii) a person who obstructs a police‑officer, escapes or attempts to escape lawful custody; (viii) a person reasonably suspected of being a deserter from the armed forces; (ix) a person involved in an act committed abroad that would be an offence in Bangladesh; (x) a released convict breaching any rule made under section 565; and (xi) a person for whose arrest a requisition has been received from another police‑officer that specifies the person and the offence. In all cases the officer must have reason to believe the person has committed the offence and must be satisfied that the arrest is necessary for investigation, prevention of further offence, preservation of evidence, or to ensure the person’s presence in court.

citations.quote: Any police-officer may, without an order from a Magistrate and without warrant, arrest- firstly, any person who commits, in the presence of a police-officer, a cognizable offence; secondly, any person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years

any person against whom credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years whether with or without fine, or with death sentence
any person having in his possession without lawful excuse, the burden of proving which excuse shall lie on such person, any implement of house breaking
any person who has been proclaimed as an offender either under this Code or by order of the Government

any person in whose possession anything is found which may reasonably be suspected to be stolen property and who may reasonably be suspected of having committed an offence with reference to such thing
any person who obstructs a police-officer while in the execution of his duty, or who has escaped, or attempts to escape, from lawful custody
any person reasonably suspected of being a deserter from the armed forces of Bangladesh

any person who has been concerned in, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made or credible information has been received or a reasonable suspicion exists of his having been concerned in, any act committed at any place out of Bangladesh, which, if committed in Bangladesh, would have been punishable as an offence
any released convict committing a breach of any rule made under section 565, sub-section

any person for whose arrest a requisition, has been received from another police-officer, provided that the requisition specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made

text: The police may detain a person arrested without a warrant for up to twenty‑four hours (excluding the time needed to travel to the Magistrate’s Court), unless a special order under section 167 is obtained.

citations.quote: shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.
take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The search of a woman must be carried out by another woman, observing strict decency.

citations.quote: Whenever it is necessary to cause a woman to be searched, the search shall be made by another woman, with strict regard to decency.

text: Only the amount of restraint that is necessary to prevent the arrested person’s escape may be used; no more restraint than that is permitted.

citations.quote: The person arrested shall not be subjected to more restraint than is necessary to prevent his escape.

text: When making an arrest a police officer must: (a) bear a clear identification of his name; (b) disclose his identity and show his identity card if asked; (c) prepare a memorandum of arrest that is attested by a suitable witness; (d) have the memorandum countersigned or thumb‑impressed by the arrested person if he does not refuse; (e) within 24 hours inform a family member, relative or nominated friend of the arrest, giving the time, place and custody details; (f) if the arrested person has any injury, arrange for medical examination and first‑aid and obtain a medical certificate; and (g) allow the arrested person, if he wishes, to consult a lawyer of his choice or meet a close relative, preferably within twelve hours.

citations.quote: bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name which will facilitate easy identification
disclose his identity and if demanded, shall show his identity card to the person arrested and to the persons present at the time of arrest
prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be- (i) attested by at least one witness, who is a member of the family of the person arrested or a respectable inhabitant of the locality
countersigned or thumb-impressed by the person arrested if not refused by him

intimate, where the accused is arrested from a place other than his residence, to a family member, relative, or a friend nominated by the person arrested, as soon as practicable but not later than twenty four hours

ensure, if any mark of injury is found on the body of the person arrested, the examination and first aid treatment of the person by a medical officer... obtain a certificate from the attending medical officer
(f) allow the person arrested, if he so desires, to consult a lawyer of his choice or to meet any of his nearest relation, preferably within twelve hours of such arrest

text: Yes. The Code of Criminal Procedure requires that a police officer inform the person being arrested of the reasons for the arrest at the time of the arrest.

citations.quote: Every police-officer arresting any person without warrant shall, at the time of making arrest, communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.

text: When information about a cognizable offence is given to the officer in charge of a police‑station, it must be reduced to writing (or written by the officer or under his direction), read back to the informant, signed by the informant, and the substance entered in a book kept by that officer in the form prescribed by the Government.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police‑station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the Government may prescribe in this behalf.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a police officer may not investigate a non‑cognizable offence unless a Magistrate first orders the investigation.

citations.quote: No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case

text: Yes. Under section 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an officer in charge of a police‑station may investigate a cognizable case without a Magistrate’s order.

citations.quote: Any officer in charge of a police-station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case

text: Yes. A police officer conducting an investigation may, by a written order, require a person who appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case to attend before him, and that person must comply.

citations.quote: may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person ... who, ... appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case; and such person shall attend as so required.

text: No. A witness is not bound to answer questions whose answers would tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture.

citations.quote: Such person shall be bound to answer all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a statement made to a police officer during an investigation must not be signed by the person making it.

citations.quote: No statement made by any person to a police-officer in the course of an investigation under this Chapter shall, if reduced into writing, be signed by the person making it;

text: No. A police officer is prohibited from offering any inducement, threat or promise to obtain a statement.

citations.quote: No police-officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in the Evidence Act, 1872, section 24.

text: A Magistrate who is a Metropolitan Magistrate, a Magistrate of the first class, or a Magistrate of the second class specially empowered by the Government (provided he is not a police‑officer) may record a confession. Before recording it, the Magistrate must explain to the person that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does, the confession may be used as evidence against him.

citations.quote: Any Metropolitan Magistrate, any Magistrate of the first class] and any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered in this behalf by the Government may, if he is not a police-officer record any statement or confession
A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him

text: If, after arrest, the police determine that the investigation cannot be finished within the 24‑hour period fixed by section 61, the officer in charge (or a police‑officer of at least sub‑inspector rank) must immediately send a copy of the diary entries to the nearest Judicial Magistrate and forward the accused to that Magistrate. The Magistrate may then authorize detention of the accused (in police custody) for up to fifteen days, but lower‑class magistrates cannot do so. The Magistrate can also order a medical examination of the accused before or after custody if there are signs of injury or an allegation of torture. For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or more than ten years, the Court of Session may, at its discretion, release the accused on bail.

citations.quote: Whenever any person is arrested and detained in custody, and it appears that the investigation cannot be completed within the period of twenty-four hours ... the officer ... shall forthwith transmit ... a copy of the entries in the diary ... and shall at the same time forward the accused to such Magistrate.

The Magistrate ... may ... authorize the detention of the accused in such custody ... for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole; ... no Magistrate of the third class ... shall authorize detention in the custody of the police.

may order that the accused be examined by a medical officer of nearest government hospital before he is handed over to such custody; ... if ... there appears to be any mark of injury ... the Magistrate shall direct that the accused be examined by a medical officer ...

the Court of Session may, if the offence to which the investigation relates is punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding ten years, release the accused on bail to the satisfaction of such Court

text: A magistrate may take cognizance of an offence (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute the offence; (b) upon a written report of such facts made by any police‑officer; or (c) upon information received from any person other than a police‑officer, or upon his own knowledge or suspicion that the offence has been committed.

citations.quote: upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence; (b) upon a report in writing of such facts made by any police-officer; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police-officer, or upon his own knowledge or suspicion, that such offence has been committed.

text: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on the basis of a complaint, he must immediately examine the complainant (and any witnesses present, if he deems it necessary) and put the substance of that examination in writing, having it signed by the complainant or witness and by the Magistrate. However, if the complaint is already in writing, the Magistrate is not required to make such an examination before transferring the case.

citations.quote: A Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall at once examine ... and the substance of the examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed ... and also by the Magistrate
when the complaint is made in writing, nothing herein contained shall be deemed to require such examination before transferring the case under section 192

text: A Magistrate may postpone issuing process against the person complained about when, on receiving a complaint of an offence he can take cognizance of (or one transferred to him), he thinks it appropriate and records the reasons in writing. He may do so to compel the attendance of the complained‑against person and either investigate the case himself or, if he is not a third‑class Magistrate, direct an inquiry or investigation by a subordinate Magistrate, a police‑officer or any other person he deems fit. This postponement is allowed provided that, unless the complaint was made by a Court, the requirements of section 200 have been complied with, and it is also permitted where the offence appears to be triable exclusively by a Court of Session.

citations.quote: may, if he thinks fit, for reasons to be recorded in writing, postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against, and either inquire into the case himself or, if he is a Magistrate other than a Magistrate of the third class, direct an inquiry or investigation to be made by any Magistrate subordinate to him, or by a police-officer, or by such other person as he thinks fit, for the purpose of ascertaining the truth of falsehood of the complaint

Provided further that where it appears to the Magistrate that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by a Court of Session, the Magistrate may postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against and may make or cause to be made an inquiry or investigation as mentioned in this sub-section for the purpose of ascertaining the truth or falsehood of the complaint.

text: A magistrate may dismiss a complaint when, after considering the complainant’s statement on oath (if any) and the result of any investigation or inquiry, he judges that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding.

citations.quote: may dismiss the complaint, if ... there is in his judgment no sufficient ground for proceeding.

text: An accused must be discharged before a charge is framed if (1) the Magistrate, after examining the record and hearing the parties, finds the charge to be groundless, and (2) the Public Prosecutor withdraws the prosecution before a charge has been framed.

citations.quote: if the Magistrate ... considers the charge to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.
if it is made before a charge has been framed, the accused shall be discharged in respect of such offence or offences;

text: If the complainant does not appear on the appointed day, the Magistrate must acquit the accused, unless the Magistrate decides to adjourn the hearing to another day.

citations.quote: the Magistrate shall, notwithstanding anything herein before contained, acquit the accused, unless for some reason he thinks proper to adjoin the hearing of the case to some other day

text: If a Magistrate is satisfied that an accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious, he must record the reasons and may direct the complainant or informant to pay compensation to the accused (or each accused). He can first call the complainant to show cause why he should not pay, or issue a summons for him to appear. If the person fails to pay, the Magistrate may also order simple imprisonment for up to thirty days (and, under other provisions of the section, up to six months).

citations.quote: if he is satisfied that the accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious ... direct that compensation ... be paid by such complainant or informant to the accused or to each or any of them.

The Magistrate may, by the order directing payment of the compensation under sub-section (2), further order that, in default of payment, the person ordered to pay such compensation shall suffer simple imprisonment for a period not exceeding thirty days.
call upon him forthwith to show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused ... or ... direct the issue of a summons to him to appear and show cause as aforesaid.

text: A Metropolitan Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class may tender a pardon to an accomplice. They may do so in the case of (i) any offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session, (ii) any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, (iii) any offence punishable under section 211 of the Penal Code with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, or (iv) any offence under sections 216A, 369, 401, 435 or 477A of the Penal Code. The power may be exercised at any stage of investigation, inquiry or trial, but when the offence is under inquiry or trial only the Chief Judicial Magistrate (or the Magistrate conducting the inquiry or trial) may use it, and when the offence is under investigation the magistrate must have jurisdiction over the place where the offence might be inquired into or tried and must have the sanction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

citations.quote: In the case of any offence triable exclusively by the [***] Court of Session, or any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, or any offence punishable under section 211 of the Penal Code, with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, or any offence under any of the following sections of the Penal Code, namely, sections 216A, 369, 401, 435 and 477A, [a Metropolitan Magistrate] or any Magistrate of the first class may, at any state of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of the offence, ... tender a pardon to such person

Provided that, where the offence is under inquiry or trial, no Magistrate of the first class other than the [Chief Judicial Magistrate] shall exercise the power ... unless he is the Magistrate making the inquiry or holding the trial, and, where the offence is under investigation, no such Magistrate shall exercise the said power unless he is a Magistrate having jurisdiction ... and the sanction of the [Chief Judicial Magistrate] has been obtained

text: An accused may be tried in his absence when the court is satisfied that he has absconded or is concealing himself and there is no immediate prospect of arrest, after a public notice has been issued and he fails to appear; when, after having appeared or being released on bail, he absconds or fails to appear again; or when the judge or magistrate is satisfied that the accused is incapable of remaining before the court and is represented by an advocate, the court may dispense with his attendance and proceed with the trial in his absence. The Code also permits the court to record witness testimony in the accused’s absence when he has absconded and cannot be arrested, which allows the trial to continue without him.

citations.quote: where the Court has reason to believe that an accused person has absconded or is concealing himself ... and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, ... if such person fails to comply ... he shall be tried in his absence
the procedure ... shall not apply and the Court ... shall, recording its decision so to do, try such person in his absence

if the Judge or Magistrate is satisfied ... that any one or more of [the] accused is or are incapable of remaining before the Court, he may, if such accused is represented by [an advocate], dispense with his attendance and proceed ... in his absence
If it is proved that an accused person has absconded, and that there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the Court ... may, in his absence, examine the witnesses

text: Yes. Under section 485 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court may imprison a person who refuses to answer questions put to him without a reasonable excuse.

citations.quote: If any witness or person ... refuses to answer such questions ... the Court may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, sentence him to simple imprisonment ...

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a criminal court is deemed an open court and the public generally may have access, subject to the judge’s power to restrict access in particular cases.

citations.quote: The place in which any Criminal Court is held for the purpose of inquiring into or trying any offence shall be deemed an open Court, to which the public generally may have access, so far as the same can conveniently contain them: Provided that the presiding Judge or Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, order at any stage of any inquiry into, or trial of, any particular case, that the public generally, or any particular person, shall not have access to, or be or remain in, the room or building used by the Court.
The word “public” includes any class of the public or any community.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a person who has been acquitted of an offence cannot be tried again for the same offence while that acquittal remains in force.

citations.quote: A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence

text: An appeal against an order of acquittal may be presented by the Government (by directing the Public Prosecutor to do so) and, where the case was instituted on a complaint and the acquittal involves an error of law, the complainant himself may present the appeal.

citations.quote: the Government may, in any case, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal- (a) to the High Court Division from an original or appellate Order of acquittal passed by any Court of Session; (b) to the Court of Session from an original or appellate Order of acquittal passed by any Magistrate.

the complainant may present an appeal- (a) to the High Court Division from an original order of acquittal passed by any Court of Session; (b) to the Court of Session from an original order of acquittal passed by any Magistrate.

text: The High Court Division may, whenever it thinks fit, issue directions to: (a) bring a person within its appellate criminal jurisdiction before the Court to be dealt with according to law; (b) set at liberty a person illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody; (c) bring a prisoner detained in any jail within its limits before the Court to be examined as a witness; (d) bring such a prisoner before a Court‑martial or Commissioners for trial or examination; (e) remove a prisoner within its limits from one custody to another for trial.

citations.quote: that a person within the limits of its appellate criminal jurisdiction be brought up before the Court to be dealt with according to law;
that a person illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody with such limits be set at liberty;
that a prisoner detained in any jail situate within such limits be brought before the Court to be there examined as a witness in any matter pending or to be inquired into in such Court;

that a prisoner detained as aforesaid be brought before a Court-martial or any Commissioners for trial or to be examined touching any matter pending before such Court-martial or Commissioners respectively;
that a prisoner within such limits be removed from one custody to another for the purpose of trial;

text: The Code does not require automatic release of a person accused of a bailable offence. Section 496 provides that such a person shall be released on bail only when he is prepared to give bail; otherwise the provision does not mandate release.

citations.quote: When any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence ... is prepared at any time while in the custody of such officer or at any stage of the proceedings ... to give bail, such person shall be released on bail

text: Bail may be granted to a person accused of a non‑bailable offence when the person is arrested or detained without a warrant, or appears before a court, provided there are no reasonable grounds to believe the person has committed an offence punishable with death or transportation for life. The court may still grant bail to a person under sixteen years of age, a woman, or a sick or infirm accused. Bail may also be granted at any stage of investigation, inquiry or trial if the officer or court finds that there are no reasonable grounds to believe the accused has committed a non‑bailable offence but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry; in that case the accused may be released on bail or on a bond without sureties. Finally, after the trial but before judgment is delivered, if the court believes there are reasonable grounds to think the accused is not guilty, the accused must be released on a bond without sureties.

citations.quote: When any person accused of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police-station, or appears or is brought before a Court he may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life: Provided that the Court may direct that any person under the age of sixteen years or any woman or any sick or infirm person accused of such an offence be released on bail.

If it appears to such officer or Court at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial, as the case may be, that there are not reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry into his guilt, the accused shall, pending such inquiry, be released on bail, or, at the discretion of such officer or Court, on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance as hereinafter provided.

If, at any time after the conclusion of the trial of a person accused of a non-bailable offence and before judgment is delivered, the Court is of opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of any such offence, it shall release the accused, if he is in custody on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance to hear judgment delivered.

text: Yes. The amount of a bail bond may be reduced, and this can be ordered by the High Court Division or the Court of Session.

citations.quote: the High Court Division or Court of Session may, in any case, whether there be an appeal on conviction or not, direct that any person be admitted to bail, or that the bail required by a police-officer or Magistrate be reduced.

text: When a trial is concluded, the court may order the disposal of any property or document produced before it (or in its custody) by destruction, confiscation, delivery to a person claiming entitlement, or any other manner it deems appropriate.

citations.quote: When an inquiry or a trial in any Criminal Court is concluded, the Court may make such order as it thinks fit for the disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or otherwise of any property or document produced before it or in its custody or regarding which any offence appears to have been committed, or which has been used for the commission of any offence.

text: The High Court Division retains the inherent power to make any orders it deems necessary to give effect to any order under the Code, to prevent abuse of the process of any Court, and otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

citations.quote: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent power of the High Court Division to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

text: A District Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the Government or the District Magistrate to act under this section, may issue such an order.

citations.quote: In cases where, in the opinion of a District Magistrate, [or any other Executive Magistrate] specially empowered by the Government or the District Magistrate to act under this section, ... such Magistrate may ... direct any person to abstain from a certain act

text: When a magistrate is satisfied, on the basis of a police report or other information, that a dispute over land or water is likely to cause a breach of the peace, he must issue a written order stating his reasons and requiring the parties to appear before his court and give written statements of their claims. The order must be served as a summons and at least one copy posted at the dispute site. The magistrate then reviews the statements, hears the parties, receives and considers any evidence, may take further evidence, and decides which party was in possession at the date of the order. If a party has been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed within two months before the order, the magistrate may treat that party as if he had been in possession. In an emergency, the magistrate may also attach the disputed property pending his decision. He may issue summons to witnesses or for production of documents at any stage, and this power does not limit his authority under section 107.

citations.quote: Whenever ... is satisfied ... that a dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace exists ... he shall make an order in writing, stating the grounds of his being so satisfied, and requiring the parties concerned ... to attend his Court ... and to put in written statements of their respective claims

A copy of the order shall be served in manner provided by this Code for the service of a summons upon such person or persons as the Magistrate may direct, and at least one copy shall be published by being affixed to some conspicuous place at or near the subject of dispute

The Magistrate shall then, without reference to the merits ... peruse the statements so put in, hear the parties, receive all such evidence as may be produced by them respectively, consider the effect of such evidence, take such further evidence (if any) as he thinks necessary

Provided that, if it appears to the Magistrate that any party has within two months ... been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed, he may treat the party so dispossessed as if he had been in possession at such date
Provided also, that if the Magistrate considers the case one of emergency, he may at any time attach the subject of dispute, pending his decision under this section
The Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, at any stage of the proceedings ... issue a summons to any witness directing him to attend or to produce any document or thing
Nothing in this section shall be deemed to be in derogation of the powers of the Magistrate to proceed under section 107

text: A Magistrate may require a person to execute a bond for keeping the peace when the Magistrate is informed (or has reason to believe) that the person is likely to commit a breach of the peace, disturb public tranquillity, or do any wrongful act that may probably occasion such a breach, and the Magistrate, in his opinion, has sufficient ground for proceeding.

citations.quote: Whenever ... is informed that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity or to do any wrongful act that may probably occasion a breach of the peace ... the Magistrate if in his opinion there is sufficient ground for proceeding may ... require such person ... to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace

text: Yes. When a police‑officer makes an arrest without a warrant, the law requires that the arrested person be taken, without unnecessary delay, before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police‑station.

citations.quote: A police-officer making an arrest without warrant shall, without unnecessary delay and subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The officer must give the subordinate a written order that specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made.

citations.quote: he shall deliver to the officer required to make the arrest an order in writing, specifying the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made.

text: Yes. Under section 51 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police‑officer may search an arrested person and seize any articles found on him, except for necessary clothing.

citations.quote: may search such person, and place in safe custody all articles, other than necessary wearing‑apparel, found upon him

text: A person arrested without a warrant may be detained for up to twenty‑four hours (excluding the time needed for travel to the Magistrate’s Court) before a Magistrate must authorize any further detention.

citations.quote: such period shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.

text: For a cognizable offence the police must put the information in writing, read it back to the informant, have it signed and enter it in the police‑station’s register, and they may investigate the case without a magistrate’s order. For a non‑cognizable offence the police only record the substance of the information in the register and must refer the informant to a magistrate; they may not investigate the case unless a magistrate first orders them to do so.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence ... shall be reduced to writing by him ... and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer
When information is given ... of a non-cognizable offence, he shall enter in a book ... the substance of such information and refer the informant to the Magistrate
No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate

text: The police must tell the arrested person the reasons for his arrest, and must put those reasons in writing at the time of the arrest.

citations.quote: communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.
the police-officer shall record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing

text:
For a bailable offence (any offence that is not a non‑bailable offence) the law requires that the accused be released on bail as soon as he is prepared to give it: “such person shall be released on bail” (section 496). The officer may also discharge him on a bond without sureties.

For a non‑bailable offence the grant of bail is discretionary. The accused “may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life” (section 497(1)). Bail may still be ordered if the officer or court finds no reasonable grounds to believe the accused committed a non‑bailable offence, allowing release on bail or on a bond without sureties (section 497(2)). After a trial but before judgment, the court may release the accused on a bond without sureties if it believes he is not guilty (section 497(4)). The High Court or Court of Session may also re‑arrest a person who was released under this section (section 497(5)).

citations.quote: such person shall be released on bail
he may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life

the accused shall, pending such inquiry, be released on bail, or, at the discretion of such officer or Court, on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance as hereinafter provided
it shall release the accused, if he is in custody on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance to hear judgment delivered

text: The extracts set out safeguards only for confessions recorded by a Magistrate. Before recording a confession, the Magistrate must tell the person that he is not obliged to confess and that any confession may be used as evidence, and must be satisfied that it was made voluntarily. If a court later finds that these procedural safeguards under section 164 were not complied with, the confession may still be admitted only if the error did not prejudice the accused’s defence. The extracts contain no specific safeguard provisions for statements made to the police.

citations.quote: A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him and ... he has reason to believe that it was made voluntarily

text: A criminal case can terminate before a full trial in several ways: (1) the public prosecutor may withdraw from the prosecution, and if the withdrawal is before a charge is framed the accused is discharged, or if after a charge is framed the accused is acquitted; (2) if a trial cannot be concluded within the statutory time limit, a non‑bailable accused may be released on bail at the court’s discretion; (3) after a trial has concluded but before judgment is delivered, the court may release a non‑bailable accused on bail if it believes the accused is not guilty; and (4) during investigation, the Court of Session may release an accused on bail for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment exceeding ten years.

text: After a person is arrested, the executive magistrate or police officer must direct the accused’s removal to the court that issued the warrant (CrPC 86). If the offence is bailable, the magistrate may take bail or security and forward the bond to that court; if it is non‑bailable, a Sessions Judge or a first‑class magistrate may release the accused on interim bail and order him to appear before the issuing court (CrPC 86). Once produced before the magistrate, the magistrate may record any statement or confession made by the accused (CrPC 164). The recorded statement is then forwarded to the magistrate who will inquire into or try the case (CrPC 164). On the date fixed for trial, the court proceeds to take all prosecution evidence (CrPC 265G). If, when the accused appears, the magistrate finds him capable of making his defence, the inquiry or trial continues (CrPC 468). If the case is transferred to another magistrate, the succeeding magistrate may act on evidence already recorded by the predecessor, or may re‑summon witnesses for further examination (CrPC 350). Finally, the court records the facts of the offence together with any statement made by the offender, the finding and the sentence (CrPC 481).

text: When a magistrate is satisfied that a complaint or information is false and either frivolous or vexatious, he may record the reasons, call upon the complainant to show cause why he should not pay compensation, or issue a summons if the complainant is absent. If payment is not made, the magistrate may order simple imprisonment for up to thirty days, and may also impose imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to one lakh taka. text: The Code of Criminal Procedure (as amended) permits a police‑officer to arrest a person without a warrant in several situations.  Section 54 authorises arrest without a magistrate’s order when: (i) a person commits a cognizable offence in the presence of the officer; (ii) a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion exists that a person has committed a cognizable offence (whether punishable with imprisonment of less than seven years or up to seven years) and the officer both believes the person is guilty and is satisfied that arrest is necessary to prevent further offence, protect evidence or prevent intimidation; (iii) a requisition has been received from another police‑officer specifying the person and the offence, showing that the person could lawfully be arrested without a warrant; (iv) the officer receives credible information that the person has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of more than seven years or death; and (v) other categories listed in the subsection (e) such as possession of house‑breaking implements, stolen property, obstruction of police, desertion, etc.  Section 54 also bars arrest for the purpose of preventive detention.  Finally, Section 54A requires that every police‑officer who arrests without a warrant must at the time of arrest communicate the reasons for the arrest to the person arrested.

text: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police officer may make an arrest without a warrant in the situations described in section 55 and section 124.
